explanations.explanation: Paul says it straight: "…Demas, in his love of this world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica." That's the reason the text gives, so I won't add any more to it. Paul doesn't say how it felt for him, but I think it stung, since Demas had been counted among his fellow workers (Philemon 1:24).

Nice guess, friend, but the text doesn't say Demas was called to preach in Thessalonica. Paul says Demas left "…in his love of this world…" A preaching call would have sounded very different from "…has deserted me…"

That would be a sad reason, friend, but Paul never says anything about a sick family member for Demas. The only reason he gives is "…his love of this world…" The one Paul does mention being left sick is Trophimus (2 Timothy 4:20), and that's a different man.

"Only Luke is with me." Paul says. Luke is the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14), and he's the one still with Paul. Three people gone, and one friend still with him. I think that friend meant a whole lot.

Silas was a real partner of Paul's in his travels (Acts 15:40), so I see why he came to mind. But in this passage Paul names a different man: "Only Luke is with me." Silas doesn't show up anywhere in these verses.
Barnabas was set apart alongside Saul, also called Paul (Acts 13:2, 9), so it's a fair guess, friend. But he's not named in this passage. Paul says, "Only Luke is with me."

explanations.answer: He is useful in the ministry
explanations.explanation: Paul has just listed who's gone, and he says only Luke is with him. Then comes the ask: "Get Mark and bring him with you…" His reason is "…he is useful to me in the ministry." I think that's a big thing for Paul to say, because it's the same Mark who has a rough spot in his history with Paul, and here Paul is asking for him by name.

explanations.answer: He has money for the trip
explanations.explanation: Paul never says a word about money here, friend. His reason for wanting Mark is that "…he is useful to me in the ministry." Not a coin gets mentioned in these verses.
Paul never brings up judges when he asks for Mark. He says Mark "…is useful to me in the ministry." That's the reason, friend, and it's a good one on its own.
Not this time, friend. Paul says, "Tychicus, however, I have sent to Ephesus." Look at that "however." It sets him apart from Demas, who deserted Paul. Tychicus went because Paul sent him.
Right, friend. Paul says, "Tychicus, however, I have sent to Ephesus." Demas left Paul, but Paul himself sent Tychicus. Different road, different reason.
Paul says, "The Lord will repay him according to his deeds." Paul doesn't say he'll do it himself. He leaves it with the Lord, and I think that's a peaceful place to leave it.
Close to home, but no. Paul doesn't hand this to the church. He says, "The Lord will repay him according to his deeds." Paying Alexander back is left with the Lord.
Paul doesn't name a court here, friend. He says, "The Lord will repay him according to his deeds." The One doing the repaying is the Lord.

explanations.answer: He has strongly opposed their message
explanations.explanation: Paul says Alexander "…has vigorously opposed our message." Notice the word "our." Paul and Timothy share this message, so a warning to be careful of the man comes with it.

explanations.answer: He has spread lies about Timothy
explanations.explanation: Paul never says anything about lies, and he doesn't say Alexander went after Timothy personally. The reason is that Alexander "…has vigorously opposed our message." The target is the message, friend.

explanations.answer: He has stirred up the city leaders
explanations.explanation: Paul says nothing about city leaders, friend. Here's the reason he gives: "…he has vigorously opposed our message." One reason, and I think Paul figured that was plenty.
Paul says, "…everyone deserted me." That's a lonely moment to stand up in front of people. I think it was a hard one, and then Paul turns to the good part, which comes right after.

Here's the turn, friend: "But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me…" Everyone else left, and the Lord stayed. The strength Paul needed came from Him, so that the message would be fully proclaimed (2 Timothy 4:17).
Good word, friend, but it isn't the one Paul uses. He says, "…everyone deserted me." For the second blank, the text says "…the Lord stood by me…", so "stood" is the fit.
"Praised" doesn't show up in these verses, friend. Paul says, "…everyone deserted me." For the second blank, it's "…the Lord stood by me…" Those are the words that fit.
"Waited" sounds reasonable, but Paul doesn't use it. He says everyone "deserted" him, and the Lord "stood by" him. Standing by someone is a lot more than waiting around.

Paul says the opposite, friend. After telling Timothy that everyone deserted him, he adds, "May it not be charged against them." That's a man asking for them to be let off. I think that's a gracious thing to say.

Right, friend. Paul says, "May it not be charged against them." Just before that he says, "At my first defense, no one stood with me, but everyone deserted me." They left him, and he still asks that it not be held against them.

Paul says the Lord strengthened him "…so that through me the message would be fully proclaimed, and all the Gentiles would hear it." Gentiles are people who aren't Jews. That's the whole reach he mentions.
Jerusalem isn't mentioned in these verses, friend. Paul says the message would be fully proclaimed "…and all the Gentiles would hear it." Gentiles are people who aren't Jews.
Paul doesn't talk about churches in Judea here. He says "…all the Gentiles would hear it." That's who the message would reach.

explanations.answer: Bring him safely into the heavenly kingdom
explanations.explanation: Paul says the Lord will rescue him from every evil action and "…bring me safely into His heavenly kingdom." Paul is looking ahead to that kingdom. Then he adds, "To Him be the glory forever and ever. Amen."

explanations.answer: Free him from his chains in this life
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't mention being freed in this life, friend. He says the Lord will rescue him "…from every evil action and bring me safely into His heavenly kingdom." The kingdom is the goal he names.

explanations.answer: Give him many more years of preaching
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't ask for more years of preaching here. He says the Lord will "…bring me safely into His heavenly kingdom." Earlier in this letter he spoke of his departure being at hand (2 Timothy 4:6).

explanations.answer: He was left sick in Miletus
explanations.explanation: Paul says, "…Trophimus I left sick in Miletus." The text doesn't say more than that. I think it's a gentle reminder that Paul's circle was dealing with real troubles.
Ephesus is where Paul sent Tychicus (2 Timothy 4:12), so I see the mix-up, friend. Trophimus is a different story. Paul says, "…Trophimus I left sick in Miletus."
Troas is where Paul left his cloak with Carpus (2 Timothy 4:13), so that name was already in the air. But Troas isn't where Paul places Trophimus. He says, "…Trophimus I left sick in Miletus."
Paul says, "Make every effort to come to me before winter." He first asked back in verse 9, and now he adds a deadline. That's the word to hold onto, friend.
Passover is a real feast (Exodus 12:11), but it's not the deadline Paul gives. He says, "Make every effort to come to me before winter." Winter is the one he names.

Harvest is a fair guess, friend, but it isn't the word Paul uses. His ask is "Make every effort to come to me before winter." Back in verse 9 that same ask ended with "quickly." Now it ends with a season.
Yes, friend. The very last words are "Grace be with you all." Right before that Paul writes, "The Lord be with your spirit." He ends the letter with grace.
Not quite. The last words of the letter are "Grace be with you all." Right before that he writes, "The Lord be with your spirit." So grace is the last thing Paul leaves them with.
